INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are nonprofit organizations that provide or
advocate for health care for youth. Amici submit this
brief collectively to bring to the Court the perspectives
of people who interact directly with the issue of minor
consent, including youth, healthcare professionals, and
organizations working to improve access to health care. 2
Youth Power Project (“YPP”) is a youth-led initiative
operating in nine states, including Texas, Tennessee, and
Florida, and fiscally sponsored by Future Incubator, a
nonprofit organization. YPP empowers and trains young
people with adverse health experiences to shape public
policy through advocacy and engagement with legislators.
YPP’s interest in this case reflects its mission to ensure
that laws governing youth health care meet the needs
and experiences of young people. With their permission,
YPP offers testimonials from its members and affiliates.
Idaho Academy of Family Physicians (“IAFP”) is a
professional organization that represents Idaho family
physicians and advocates for their patients and for policies
that improve Idahoans’ health. IAFP’s interest in this case
reflects its work to preserve physicians’ ability to provide
appropriate care to minors consistent with professional
standards and applicable laws.

SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Every state has enacted laws allowing minors, in
certain circumstances, to obtain some forms of health care
without parental consent. Every day, children and youth
across the country rely on these laws to access essential
care, sometimes during urgent or life-endangering
situations. These laws, known as minor consent laws,
reflect legislatures’ careful judgments about when minors

3
can obtain care such as outpatient mental health treatment,
emergency care, and treatment for sexually transmitted
infections (“STIs”) in circumstances where requiring
parental consent would harm youth’s health and safety. 3
The minor consent law that Petitioners challenge—Wash.
Rev. Code § 71.34.530 (“RCW § 71.34.530”), which allows
youth to consent to outpatient mental health care—is
not novel. Like its counterparts in many other States,
RCW § 71.34.530 is vital to youth health and safety. The
testimonials of youth and healthcare providers presented
here show that these laws, common across the country, are
necessary for youth well-being and, at times, lifesaving. 4
Amici’s experience with these laws illustrates why
Article III does not permit standing to Petitioners.
Children and youth experience concrete harm when
they cannot access health care without parental consent.
Petitioners, by contrast, have suffered no legal harm
from RCW § 71.34.530. A parent’s interest in a child’s
upbringing, while very important, does not relieve
Petitioners from showing a concrete, traceable injury

ARGUMENT
I. Minor Consent Laws Have an Extensive History
and Have Been Adopted by All States.
A. State Supreme Courts and Legislatures Have
Long Recognized the Need for Minor Consent.
Minor consent is a well-established feature of the
law, not a new development. Under the common law, U.S.
courts have long allowed minors with sufficient maturity
to give independent consent to medical treatment in some
situations. See, e.g., Cardwell v. Bechtol , 724 S.W.2d 739,
744-45 (Tenn. 1987) (surveying case law since 1845 and
concluding the “recognition that minors achieve varying
degrees of maturity and responsibility (capacity) has
been part of the common law for well over a century”);
Gulf & S.I.R. Co. v. Sullivan, 119 So. 501, 502 (Miss. 1928)
(permitting a seventeen-year-old of “sufficient intelligence
to understand and appreciate the consequences of the
vaccination” to consent to a measles vaccination); Smith
v. Seibly, 431 P .2d 719 (Wash. 1967) (upholding consent
to medical procedure by a minor who was then a married
father).
Over decades, under what came to be known as
the mature minor doctrine, many state supreme courts
recognized the importance of minor consent in situations
where the requirement of parental consent would delay
or deny youth’s access to timely medical care. See, e.g.,

5
Younts v. St. Francis Hosp. & Sch. of Nursing, Inc. , 469
P .2d 330, 332 (Kan. 1970) (allowing a seventeen-year-old
to consent to treatment for a finger injury suffered while
visiting her mother in the hospital after her mother’s
“major surgery” that day); Cardwell, 724 S.W.2d at 748-49
(permitting a seventeen-year-old to independently consent
to treatment for back pain).
Beginning in the 1950s, many states passed legislation
adopting minor consent laws. 5 These statutes allowed
minors to consent to select types of health care essential
to youth health and safety, such as emergency care,
substance-use disorder treatment, prenatal care, and
sexual assault examination; or authorized medical
providers to offer such care to youth without parental
consent. By 1972, forty-three states had passed laws
allowing minors to access STI testing and treatment
without parental consent, and twenty-five states had
permitted qualifying minors to access pregnancy-related
care and substance-use disorder treatment without
parental consent. 6
Contrary to Petitioners’ assertion, 7 permitting minor
consent in certain cases does not displace the general

(“Adoption of the mature minor exception to the common
law rule is by no means a general license to treat minors
without parental consent . . . .”). Rather, minor consent laws,
including RCW § 71.34.530, supplement and complement
the general requirement of parental consent by carving
out exceptions where requiring parental consent would
hinder, rather than facilitate, youth’s access to medical
care. Empirical data confirms that despite the prevalence
of minor consent laws, most minors still involve parents in
their health care decisions.8 And even where youth access
care through minor consent, many ultimately involve their
parents and family in their health care, often with the
encouragement and support of healthcare professionals.
While minor consent opens the door to care, it does not
close the door on parents. 9 See infra Part II.B.

were accessing sexual health services at the clinic”).

govern who may authorize care. Separate federal and state laws
typically govern disclosure of information. Many permit or require

B. Every State Has Adopted Some Form of Minor
Consent Laws.
Today, all fifty states have passed some form of minor
consent laws to ensure youth access to certain types of
essential health care.10 As shown in the chart in Appendix
2, among all fifty states, forty-nine allow certain minors
access to STI testing and treatment without parental
consent; forty-eight to substance-use services; forty-five
to emergency care; thirty-nine to prenatal care; thirtyfive to outpatient mental health care; and twenty-four to
sexual assault examination.
Although these laws differ by state, 11 they share
one basic consensus—for youth health and safety, it is
necessary in some situations to allow youth to access
health care without parental consent. Indeed, even where
state legislatures have recently passed laws limiting youth
access to health care without parental consent, legislatures
still acknowledge the need for some exceptions.
In 2022, Florida passed House Bill 817 to authorize
emergency care for minors without parental consent.
Act of Apr. 6, 2022, ch. 2022-53, 2022 Fla. Laws (codified
at Fla. Stat. § 743.064(1)). The legislature’s bill analysis
explicitly named Florida’s “obligation to ensure that
children receive reasonable medical treatment that is

The nationwide consensus in favor of minor consent

minors cannot access care independently. In one example,
a youth patient came to her walk-in clinic several times
over a period of weeks with abdominal pain. Her mother
declined to allow Dr. Pyrak to speak with her daughter
alone, and the youth patient did not answer when asked
about her sexual history in front of her mother. On the
youth’s fourth visit, the minor “had a fever and [Dr. Pyrak]
became more alarmed, and was finally at that point allowed
to do an abdominal exam and speak with the youth alone.
We found that she had an untreated chlamydia infection
that had progressed to Pelvic Inflammatory Disease,
which can impact a patient’s fertility. If the youth had
gotten testing and treatment for the chlamydia earlier, she
would not have developed PID and its associated risks.”

28
f. Parental Consent Requirements Can
Obstruct Substance-Use Treatment.
Clinicians treating adolescents for substance-use
disorders ordinarily try to involve parents. But for
some teenagers, requiring notification at the outset can
keep them from seeking help. During a 2024 debate
over broader parental consent requirements in New
Hampshire, licensed drug and alcohol counselor Jacqui
Abikoff explained that some minors will seek help only
if their parents will not immediately be notified. New
Hampshire ultimately left in place a statute allowing
minors twelve and older to seek drug-dependency
treatment without parental consent. 43
Parental unavailability can also interrupt care already
underway. At a 2023 California legislative hearing,
pediatrician Jayme Congdon described a seventeen-yearold patient, “CB,” who had, with her mother’s support,
begun buprenorphine treatment while hospitalized for
opioid withdrawal. But before her outpatient appointment,
her mother—who also had an opioid use disorder—
relapsed and left home. Without parental consent, the
clinicians could not continue CB’s medication. “She
showed up several times without her mother,” Dr. Congdon
testified, and without access to care, CB eventually
relapsed.44

g. Youth Can Be Denied Basic Health Care
in School.
Sweeping parental consent laws can and have denied
youth basic health care in school. Under such laws, school
nurses have been unable to provide basic treatments to
students who lack parental consent on file, due to confusion
and fear of potential legal violations.45 For instance, after
passage of S.B. 1329, some Idaho school employees were
unable to treat a student with a broken femur because
they could not contact his parents. 46 In Florida, schools
now must call parents to pick up injured or sick children
who lack parental consent on file, and educators are
prohibited from providing even bandages or ice packs to
these students.47 Likewise, a boy in Texas was sent home
covered in vomit because school staff believed they could

III. Petitioners Have No Concrete Injury Traceable to
RCW § 71.34.530 That Could Give Them Standing
to Challenge It.
The Constitution only extends the federal judicial
power to “Cases” and “Controversies.” U.S. Const. art.
III, § 2. That limit confines federal courts to redressing or
preventing actual or imminent injury. Summers v. Earth
Island Inst., 555 U.S. 488, 492 (2009). Article III standing
enforces that limit, and its core is “an essential and
unchanging part of the case-or-controversy requirement
. . . .” Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife , 504 U.S. 555, 560
(1992).
Disagreement with a legislature’s decisionmaking is
not, by itself, a substitute for the concrete injury Article
III requires. Standing is a “bedrock constitutional
requirement.” FDA v. All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S.
367, 378 (2024). The Court has “repeatedly held that mere
offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a
concrete and particularized injury under Article III.”
Nat’l Park Serv. v. Nat’l Tr. for Historic Pres. in the
United States , 609 U.S. ____ (2026) (per curiam) (slip
op. at 3). Petitioners describe only their disagreement
with Washington State allowing some youth to access
outpatient behavioral health care; they fail to articulate
any concrete injury from this law. Article III standing
prevents litigants like Petitioners from litigating their
displeasure with policies that do not harm them. See, e.g.,
id. (collecting cases and reiterating that genuine interest
does not alone satisfy the “particular concrete injury”
requirement); Valley Forge Christian Coll. v. Ams. United
for Separation of Church & State, Inc. , 454 U.S. 464, 485
(1982) (standing is not satisfied by “the psychological

32
consequence presumably produced by observation of
conduct with which one disagrees . .  .  ”) . Petitioners’
standing theories all fail because Petitioners can show
no current or plausible future harm and Petitioners are
not the objects of the challenged laws. Amici address
three points specific to Petitioners’ challenges to RCW
§ 71.34.530.
First, Petitioners are not the object of RCW
§ 71.34.530. Petitioners contend that “all Washington
parents of children ages 13-17 who would oppose ‘outpatient
treatment’ for their child without parental authorization
are . . . the object of RCW §71.34.530,” and would
therefore have standing. Pet’rs Br. at 30. However, this
Court has held that, when an alleged injury arises from
the government’s regulation of someone else, standing is
“substantially more difficult” to establish. Lujan, 504 U.S.
at 562 (quoting Allen v. Wright, 468 U.S. 737, 758 (1984)).
RCW § 71.34.530 does not regulate parents or require
them to do, refrain from doing, or permit anything. It
instead regulates the circumstances in which minors
and treatment providers may proceed without a parent’s
consent: a minor age thirteen or older “may request
and receive outpatient treatment without the consent of
the adolescent’s parent.” RCW § 71.34.530. The statute
operates on the minor’s ability to obtain treatment and
the provider’s ability to furnish it, not on the parent. That
does not, of course, make parental interests irrelevant. It
means only that Article III requires a parent challenging
the statute to identify a concrete injury caused by it.
Second, Petitioners’ own briefing makes clear that
they experience no injury from RCW § 71.34.530.
Their petition presented a single  question: “Whether

33
parents have standing to challenge a law or policy that
deliberately displaces their decisionmaking role as to
‘gender transitions’ of their children. . . .” See Pet. for Writ
of Cert. at i. However, RCW § 71.34.530 does not address
gender-affirming medical interventions. Id. It is a general
behavioral health statute limited to outpatient treatment.
Resp. Br. 12-14.
Further, Petitioners’ Merits Brief asserts that only
Parents 5A and 5B have standing to challenge RCW
§ 71.34.530 based on current harms. Pet’rs Br. at 44-45.
But their child is now an adult, so their claims are moot.
Resp. Br. 16, 21, 36. And the operative complaint does
not allege that their child’s subsequent hospitalizations
were outpatient treatment under RCW § 71.34.530, that
5A and 5B declined to authorize it, or that they sought
information from the child’s providers. First Amended
Complaint (“FAC”) ¶¶ 55-57 ( Pet. App. 77a). Any alleged
future harm for other Petitioners depends on the choices
of independent third parties and is too speculative to
support standing. Resp. Br. 41-47.
Third, Petitioners have conceded that RCW
§ 71.34.530 poses “zero” risk of constitutional harm
to them. Washington’s law has permitted adolescents
thirteen and older to obtain outpatient treatment without
parental consent, in substantially similar form, since
1985. Pet. App. 5a. Petitioners’ Complaint attributes their
asserted risk of constitutional harm entirely to the 2023
amendments to the shelter law, a different statute also
challenged by Petitioners: “Before the… amendments, the
probability of constitutional injuries here was zero—the
threat is entirely due to the statute’s amendments, thus
satisfying traceability. And so, holding unconstitutional

34
the… amendments will entirely redress the threat of
injury.” FAC ¶ 148  (emphasis added). 50 By Petitioners’
own account, then, RCW § 71.34.530, in effect for nearly
four decades before those amendments, offers “zero”
risk of constitutional harm to them. FAC ¶ 148. Because
a plaintiff must clearly allege facts establishing standing,
that concession is dispositive. Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578
U.S. 330, 338 (2016).
50. For the reasons Respondents explain, Petitioners also do
not have standing to challenge the 2023 amendments. See Resp.
Br. 30–49.
